content.question: Two selectors find the same Submit button. One breaks when a developer renames a CSS class. Which one survives a refactor?

content.prompt: Write a Playwright test that navigates to 'https://demo.playwright.dev/todomvc' and verifies the page title contains 'TodoMVC'. Use the test() function with async/await.
content.hint: Every Playwright test callback must be `async` and use `await` for page operations because browser actions take time to complete.
content.expectedOutput: The test function takes a string name and an async callback that destructures `{ page }`. Inside, `await page.goto(url)` navigates, and `await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/TodoMVC/)` verifies the title. Without `await`, the test would finish before the browser even starts loading.

content.text: Think of `async/await` like ordering food at a restaurant. When you say `await page.goto(url)`, you're telling the waiter "I'll wait here until the page is ready." Without `await`, it's like shouting your order and immediately asking "where's my food?" — the kitchen hasn't even started yet. The `async` keyword on the function is like making a reservation — it tells JavaScript "this function will have waiting involved, prepare for it." Selectors like `getByRole` are like describing what you want to the waiter: "the button that says Submit" works even if they rearrange the menu (change CSS classes). But saying "item #47" (CSS ID) breaks the moment they reprint the menu.

content.annotation: Line 3 — `async ({ page })` destructures the test fixtures; `page` is a fresh browser tab. Line 6-7 — `getByPlaceholder` finds the input by its placeholder attribute, which is how screen readers identify it too. Line 12 — `getByText` finds any element containing that exact text. Notice every `page` interaction uses `await` because the browser is a separate process — these operations are asynchronous promises that resolve when the browser completes the action.

content.modification: Remove the `await` keyword from line 4 (`page.goto(...)`) so it becomes just `page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/todomvc');`
content.question: What happens when you remove await from page.goto()?
options: The test passes but runs slower
The test fails because the page hasn't loaded when it tries to find the heading
The test throws a syntax error at compile time
content.explanation: Without `await`, `page.goto()` returns a Promise but doesn't wait for it to resolve. The code immediately moves to line 5 and tries to find a heading on a page that hasn't loaded yet. The locator finds nothing, `toBeVisible()` times out after 5 seconds, and the test fails with a timeout error. This is the #1 beginner mistake in Playwright — forgetting `await` on async operations.

content.label: getByRole vs CSS Selectors — Resilience to change
content.question: A developer changes the button's class from 'submit' to 'btn-primary' and its ID from 'login-btn' to 'auth-button'. How many tests break in each approach?
options: Code A breaks on 2 lines — Code B breaks on 0 lines
Code A breaks on 1 line — Code B breaks on 1 line
content.explanation: Code A uses CSS selectors tied to implementation details (IDs, classes, DOM structure). When `#login-btn` becomes `#auth-button`, line 1 breaks. When `.submit` becomes `.btn-primary`, line 3 breaks. Code B uses semantic locators based on what the USER sees — the button text "Log in" and "Submit" didn't change, so zero tests break. This is why Playwright recommends `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByText` — they mirror how real users (and screen readers) find elements.

content.sentence: The _____ keyword marks a function as returning a Promise, while _____ pauses execution until that Promise resolves, and _____ finds elements by their accessible role instead of CSS implementation details.

content.text: You can now write tests that find elements reliably. But finding elements is only half the story — you need to VERIFY what you found is correct. Unit 3 introduces assertions (`expect`) that auto-retry, plus TypeScript interfaces to structure your test data so your tests are both reliable and maintainable.
content.note: The locator strategies you just learned (getByRole, getByText, getByPlaceholder) will be used in every single test from now on. Master them now — they're the foundation of everything that follows. Practice by inspecting a real website and identifying elements by their role, label, and text rather than their CSS class.
